sections.html:
The Recorder of Deeds is in the Dauphin County Courthouse, Room 102, 101 Market Street, Harrisburg. The counter is staffed weekdays from eight until half past four, and the phone is (717) 780-6560.

Anything filed against Dauphin County land goes through this counter or its online equivalent: deeds, mortgages, satisfactions, easements, plans and powers of attorney. The office records, reproduces and indexes documents the law allows to be recorded. Title advice is outside its role.

If you sell through a title company, you will rarely deal with the office yourself. The settlement agent prepares the deed, adds the fees and transfer tax, and sends it in.

A deed and a mortgage each carry an $87.75 fee on the schedule revised December 1, 2025. Any document that needs a Unified Parcel Identifier adds $20.00 for each identifier.

Dauphin County recording fees by document
DocumentRecording fee
Deed$87.75
Mortgage$87.75
Satisfaction of mortgage$59.75
Assignment of mortgage$59.75
Easement$59.75
Right of way$58.75
Power of attorney$18.50
Notary filing of commission$33.50
Plan, first page$20.50

A page past the fourth costs $2.00, and a name past the ninth costs fifty cents. Simple instruments such as affidavits, agreements, releases and notices run $18.50.

The Commonwealth sets these fees through the General Assembly, and they can change. A fee calculator on the office web page works out the total for a given document.

A 2% levy applies to what is paid for the property. One point goes to the Department of Revenue, with a half point apiece for the township or borough and the school district.

Both parties to a deed share liability for the state's portion, and the recorder forwards it. The purchase agreement is where buyer and seller decide who pays.

  • Conveyances between spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, and brothers and sisters are exempt, and other exemptions exist in special cases.
  • A deed for nominal consideration, such as $1, between tax exempt parties carries $0 of transfer tax and does not need separate checks.
  • State law also exempts property passed by will or by intestate succession, burial site deeds and certain transfers to governments.

Have the settlement agent confirm the final tax figure before closing, since it depends on the price.

For most sales the path looks like this. At closing you sign the deed in front of a notary. The settlement agent then works out the recording fee, adds $20.00 for each parcel identifier, calculates the transfer tax from the price and writes the checks. The package goes to Room 102, and the recorded original returns to the agent in a day or two.

If you are selling on your own, call (717) 780-6560 first, confirm the total for your page and name count, and bring a check made out to the Dauphin County Recorder of Deeds. Keep the receipt. A cash sale changes nothing here, because the same deed, fees and tax apply whether or not a lender is involved.

After recording, ask the agent for a copy of the deed. You can also search the online index later to see that the new owner's name now appears.

sections.h2: Paying fees and getting the original back
sections.html:
Cash and checks are the accepted payment methods, and checks name the Dauphin County Recorder of Deeds. Mailed packages need a stamped return envelope with your address and the correct amount.

The original usually comes back to whoever presented it within a day or two, though busy periods, holidays and staffing can stretch that. If two weeks pass with nothing in hand, ask the firm that filed it.

Large closings often go through a title company, so ask which firm will submit the deed and how it will pay.

The first recorded registry dates to 1785. The office website holds deeds and miscellaneous documents from 1785 forward and mortgages from 1979 forward, and the deed indexes and a mortgage index are online under the Alpha Index.

Each document is scanned, and the original is held until at least two people have checked and proofed the indexes and records. Images are backed up to hard drive and microfilmed to meet Pennsylvania Historical Museum Commission requirements. The microfilm is stored off-site in an underground facility so records can be rebuilt after a courthouse disaster.

Nearly everything recorded is public. The exception is a military discharge paper, DD214. Search access requires accepting the office's disclaimer, which states that the official records are the ones held in the office.

New notaries start here. Bring identification, the completed notary bond and payment. The office records the bond and commission and administers the oath, and the notary then walks to the Prothonotary to register a signature. No appointment is needed, and the filing fee is $33.50.

The office also takes plans at $20.50 for the first page and $5.00 for each page after, and files Uniform Commercial Code statements at $100.00. Certified copies cost $2.00 plus the per page copy charge. Microfilm copies are $0.75 and photocopies are $0.50 a page.

Burial plots confuse people. A cemetery lot deed usually grants permission to use the ground while the cemetery keeps title, and those papers are held by the cemetery company or association rather than the county.

sections.h2: Questions that come up before a sale
sections.html:
A few questions repeat at the counter.

  • A change of ownership needs a new deed prepared and recorded. Merely stating a change does nothing.
  • After a mortgage is paid, the lender typically sends a satisfaction to the office. The owner does not get a new deed.
  • If a spouse dies and the couple held title as tenants by the entirety, the survivor generally explains the death in the next deed or mortgage. Other forms of title, such as tenants in common, may need different handling, so ask an attorney.
  • A deed for a lot usually covers buildings erected on it, now or later.
  • A deed gives a legal description of boundaries, but a surveyor places markers on the ground.

Anyone can write their own deed, though an attorney is the safer choice so the recording criteria are met and the right fee is enclosed.

The county had an estimated 293,351 people in July 2025, up from 286,401 in the 2020 count, and 129,660 housing units. For 2020 to 2024 the median owner-occupied home value is $236,400, and owners occupy 63.1% of homes. Median gross rent is $1,217, median household income is $76,242, and 329 building permits were issued in 2025.

faqs.q: What will a Dauphin County deed cost to record?
faqs.a: The deed fee is $87.75 on the December 1, 2025 revision, with $20.00 added for each Unified Parcel Identifier and $2.00 for every page after the fourth. Transfer tax is figured separately from the sale price.

faqs.q: What transfer tax rate applies in Dauphin County?
faqs.a: The rate is 2% of the value conveyed, divided as 1% for the state and a half percent each for the municipality and school district. Some transfers between close relatives are exempt.

faqs.q: Does the Recorder of Deeds accept cards?
faqs.a: Cash and checks are the listed payment methods for recording fees. Make checks payable to Dauphin County Recorder of Deeds, and phone (717) 780-6560 before relying on any other method.

faqs.q: When does a recorded deed come back to me?
faqs.a: Usually within one to two days, though volume, holidays and staffing can add time. After two weeks without your papers, contact whoever submitted them.

faqs.q: Can I search Dauphin County deeds online?
faqs.a: Yes. The office website has deeds and miscellaneous documents from 1785 and mortgages from 1979, searchable after you accept a disclaimer. Military discharge papers are the one category closed to the public.
